say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today we are on a farm and in a bicycle shop. We will count legs and wheels, line things up in neat rows called arrays, and share things out fairly.
Our big question today: when there are two kinds of things mixed up, how can we find out how many of each there are, without guessing wildly?
Here are some cards. Each card shows some cars, bicycles or animals. Count the wheels or the legs. Count in 2s, 3s, 4s or 5s, not in 1s!
Show me the number with your fingers or on your whiteboard. Then we will click to check.
The farmer has only hens and goats in a pen. He counts 16 legs. How many animals do you think there are? Is there only one answer? Write a guess.
stuck: Stuck: try all hens first. How many hens make 16 legs?
Then swap one hen for a goat. What happens to the number of legs? Fix it.
Finished early: which mix has the most animals? Which has the fewest? How do you know there are no more mixes?

say: "3 rows of 4 dots. I count the rows: 3. I count how many in each row: 4. 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12. If I turn my head, it is 4 rows of 3, so 4 × 3 = 12 too. Sharing 12 into 3 rows gives 4 in each row: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Putting 12 in groups of 4 gives 3 groups: 12 ÷ 4 = 3."
"Part of this tray is under a cloth. I do not need to see every cookie. The top row shows 5 in each row. The side shows 4 rows. 4 rows of 5 is 20. I can see 8, so 20 − 8 = 12 are hidden."

"6 vehicles, bicycles and cars, 16 wheels. I start with all bicycles: 6 bicycles is 12 wheels. Too few. I swap one bicycle for a car: that adds 2 wheels, 14. Swap again: 16. So 4 bicycles and 2 cars. Check: 8 + 8 = 16 wheels, 4 + 2 = 6 vehicles."

do: Ask: "How many rows? How many in each row? Which multiplication is that?"
Ask: "What changes each time you swap one animal for the other kind?"
Ask: "Did you check BOTH clues: the number of animals and the number of legs?"
stuck: Hint 1: "Draw it. Dots in rows, or circles for heads and sticks for legs."
Hint 2: "Start with all of one kind. Then swap one at a time."
Hint 3: "Make a table so you can see the pattern and do not miss a row."

do: Ask: "How many rows? How many in each row? Which multiplication is that?"
Ask: "What changes each time you swap one animal for the other kind?"
Ask: "Did you check BOTH clues: the number of animals and the number of legs?"
stuck: Hint 1: "Draw it. Dots in rows, or circles for heads and sticks for legs."
Hint 2: "Start with all of one kind. Then swap one at a time."
Hint 3: "Make a table so you can see the pattern and do not miss a row."

say: "Ravi shares stickers equally among 4 friends. Can the number left over ever be 4 or more?"
ask: "Ravi shares stickers equally among 4 friends. Can the number left over ever be 4 or more?"
No. If 4 or more were left, Ravi could give each friend one more, so the leftover is always 0, 1, 2 or 3.

say: "Today you drew arrays, made tables and checked both clues. Next time a puzzle has two kinds of things mixed up, start with all of one kind and swap one at a time."

p2l3-title.note: Objective: Read an array as rows of equal groups and write two multiplication and two division sentences for it; solve "how many of each" legs and wheels puzzles with a table; share with leftovers and decide what the leftover means; find all the arrays for a number. Tables used: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 only. Level note: sharing with leftovers (Q4, Q5) is division with a remainder, which is a P3 topic. It is a natural lead-in, so say "3 left over" in words and do not write remainders as "r 3". Thinking strategies taught today: DRAW IT (arrays, plates, boats) and MAKE A TABLE (start with all of one kind, swap one at a time; guess and check). Materials: About 30 counters per pair, mini whiteboards, squared paper. Optional picture cards of hens and goats, bicycles and tricycles. Online: Each child has 30 small objects (buttons, beans or Lego bricks) and a whiteboard or paper; children hold arrays and tables up to the camera. Time plan: opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6, warm-up 6 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 23.5, mini-lesson 23.5 to 35.5, brain break 35.5 to 38.5, worksheet page 1 38.5 to 52.5, check together, page 1 52.5 to 55, short teaching 55 to 59.5, worksheet page 2 59.5 to 71, check together, page 2 71 to 73.5, flex (spare time) 73.5 to 76.5, talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit ticket 81.5 to 86.5, looking back 86.5 to 88.5, closing and stamps 88.5 to 90. The Think harder and Go further slides are optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Kit ready at minute 0: ask families to put every item on the desk before the lesson starts (a 30-second check at the start).

p2l3-precheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6. Sneak-peek puzzles: two puzzles on the key idea of today, which the children have NOT learnt yet. Say out loud (about 28 words): "Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Show your paper to me only." Question 1 is an access question: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win (about 45 seconds). Question 2 is the thinking question (about 90 seconds). Then about 2 minutes for the answers slide and the move on. Answers are PRIVATE: each child holds their own paper to the camera for you only, or writes it on their own paper and shows only you on camera. Do not raise whiteboards together, do not read answers out, do not name children. Q1 answer: 15 counters (3 rows of 5: 5, 10, 15). Listen for: Counting in 5s, or drawing and counting. This is a first win for everyone. Q2 answer: 2 cars and 4 scooters (8 + 8 = 16). Listen for: Starting with all scooters (12 wheels) and swapping one at a time is the idea of today. A child who draws 6 vehicles and counts wheels is thinking well. Guess and check is welcome. At the end click to show the answers as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what. Ask only for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?" Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Children can move either way at any time. Everyone joins explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.

p2l3-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Legs and wheels count, three cards only. Point to one card at a time. Children count in 2s and 4s (not in 1s) and show the number on fingers or a whiteboard, then you click to show the answer (clicks reveal the cards in order: cars, hens, bicycles). Answers: 4 cars 16 wheels; 6 hens 12 legs; 5 bicycles 10 wheels. (Spare cards, not shown: 3 tricycles 9 wheels; 5 dogs 20 legs; 2 cars and 1 bicycle 10 wheels.) Ask: "Which times table did you use for the cars?" (4s). "For the hens and the bicycles?" (2s). Watch for children counting every wheel in 1s; ask them to point to each car and count "4, 8, 12, 16". A game of about 2.5 minutes: stop it on the clock even if the game is not finished.

p2l3-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 10.5. Read each one aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show. Answers: 15 and 10. For question 2 ask: "Is that a multiplication or a division?" (division: sharing). Spare questions in the guide table: 4 groups of 4 is 16; 30 shared by 10 children is 3 each; how many 5s make 35 is 7. Ask quick questions 1 and 3 only (about 2 minutes): children answer by thumbs, hands, not by naming a child. The other questions are spare.

p2l3-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 19.5. Pairs use counters: 2 counters stand for a hen's legs, 4 for a goat's, or they draw circles for heads and sticks for legs. Ask for a prediction first: "Is there only one answer?" Do not show a method yet; let them try. Push any child who would like more: "How do you know you have them all?" Online: children draw on paper and hold it up. The 5 mixes are in the next slide's notes. Go further (a second what-if, so nobody waits) is the box at the foot of this slide; the question is also posted in the chat when the pairs go to their breakout rooms. It is for ANY child who finishes the explore task or wants more: say it to the whole group as a choice, never as a prize, and never name who tries it. Pairs stay together unless both children agree to split. Answer: 6 mixes: 10 hens; 8 hens and 1 goat; 6 hens and 2 goats; 4 hens and 3 goats; 2 hens and 4 goats; 5 goats. Take it at the debrief only if a pair offers it.

p2l3-explore2.note: Minutes 19.5 to 23.5. Gather the pairs and take answers. Write the mixes on the board IN ORDER of goats: 0 goats and 8 hens; 1 goat and 6 hens; 2 goats and 4 hens; 3 goats and 2 hens; 4 goats and 0 hens. That is 5 mixes (4 if the pen must have both kinds; accept either if the child says which). Answers: 1) 5 mixes. 2) The goats go 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; 5 goats would need 20 legs, too many. 3) The legs stay at 16: 2 hens have 4 legs, the same as 1 goat. Say: "Going in order made sure we did not miss one. Today we use tables to go in order." Keep it moving (about 4 minutes in all): ask "how do you know?" on question 2 only; about 15 seconds of talk on the other questions.

p2l3-teach1.note: Minutes 23.5 to 26. Teach. Build 3 rows of 4 counters while the children copy. Click to reveal each step. Think-aloud: "3 rows of 4 dots. I count the rows: 3. I count how many in each row: 4. 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12. If I turn my head, it is 4 rows of 3, so 4 × 3 = 12 too. Sharing 12 into 3 rows gives 4 in each row: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Putting 12 in groups of 4 gives 3 groups: 12 ÷ 4 = 3." Ask: "One array, how many number sentences?" (four: two × and two ÷). Say: "An array is a DRAW IT tool: it shows the groups so we can see the times table."

p2l3-we1.note: Minutes 26 to 29. Click to reveal each step. Think-aloud: "Part of this tray is under a cloth. I do not need to see every cookie. The top row shows 5 in each row. The side shows 4 rows. 4 rows of 5 is 20. I can see 5 on top and 3 more down the side, that is 8. So 20 − 8 = 12 are hidden." Ask before step 3: "Did I count the corner cookie twice?" (No: 5 on top, then only the 3 BELOW it.) Common mistake: 5 + 4 = 9 seen, which counts the corner twice.

p2l3-teach2.note: Minutes 29 to 32.5. Teach. Click: the first note, then each table row, then the swap note and the answer (or reveal the rows as the children call them out). Think-aloud: "6 vehicles, bicycles and cars, 16 wheels. I start with all bicycles: 6 bicycles is 12 wheels. Too few. I swap one bicycle for a car: a car has 2 more wheels than a bicycle, so that adds 2 wheels, 14. Swap again: 16. So 4 bicycles and 2 cars. Check BOTH clues: 8 + 8 = 16 wheels, 4 + 2 = 6 vehicles." Say: "This is MAKE A TABLE. It is also guess and check, but tidy: every row is a guess, and the table shows us the pattern so we know which way to go."

p2l3-try2.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34.5. Whiteboards, then click. a) 4 hens = 8 legs; swap 1: 10 legs, so 3 hens and 1 goat. b) 5 bicycles = 10 wheels; each swap to a tricycle adds 1 wheel; 2 swaps make 12, so 3 bicycles and 2 tricycles. Ask about b: "Why does each swap add only 1 this time?" (3 − 2 = 1). Two items only: the stools and chairs item is dropped, the worksheet has the same type.

p2l3-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Counting the hidden part of an array one by one, or counting the corner twice, instead of rows × number in each row minus the ones you can see. (2) Giving the number of whole groups when the leftover still needs a place (28 children, vans of 5: writing 5 vans instead of 6). (3) In "how many of each" puzzles, matching the legs but forgetting to check the number of animals.

p2l3-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 38.5. Three minutes: two of movement, one for a drink of water. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place. Count the totals aloud together: 12 claps, 10 jumps, 20 stomps.

p2l3-ws1.note: Minutes 38.5 to 52.5. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. In Q3 check that pairs start with 7 hens and swap one at a time. Say once, to everyone: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never say who is on which page. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Pairs are not split unless both children agree.

p2l3-ws1ans.note: Minutes 52.5 to 55. Click each answer after a pair explains. Q2: 3 rows of 10 is 30; we can see 10 on top and 2 more down the side, 12; 30 − 12 = 18. Q3 table: 7, 0, 14; 6, 1, 16; 5, 2, 18; 4, 3, 20. Each swap adds 2 legs. Check: 4 + 3 = 7 animals.

p2l3-teachshare.note: Minutes 55 to 57. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Act it out with 17 counters and 3 paper plates: deal one to each plate per round, counting 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Click: the plates, then each step, then the note. Think-aloud: "After 5 rounds each child has 5 and I have used 15. 2 are left. Can I do another round? No: I need 3 for a round." Ask: "Could the leftover ever be 3 or more when we share among 3?" (No: then we could do another round.)

p2l3-teachround.note: Minutes 57 to 58.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Click: the boats picture, the steps, the answer. Say: "In sharing, the leftover is left over. But here every child must ride, so the leftover child needs one more boat." Ask: "How many empty seats are in the 4th boat?" (3). Compare: "17 sweets among 3 children: how many EACH?" (5, 2 left over) and "13 children, boats of 4: how many BOATS?" (4). Read the question to know what to do with the leftover.

p2l3-teachall.note: Minutes 58.5 to 59.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Use 12 counters to build each array as you click each row. Think-aloud: "2 rows: 12 shared into 2 rows is 6 in each row. 3 rows: 3, 6, 9, 12, that is 4 in each row. 4 rows of 3. 5 rows: 5, 10, 15, I jump over 12, so no. 6 rows of 2. 7 rows would need 14 chairs for 2 in each row, so I stop." Answer: 4 ways (2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4, 4 rows of 3, 6 rows of 2). Ask: "Are 3 rows of 4 and 4 rows of 3 different?" (Yes for chairs in a hall: the rows look different. On the worksheet we count them as different ways.)

p2l3-ws2.note: Minutes 59.5 to 71. Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Bicycles and tricycles with 17 wheels (find ALL the ways) is Think harder 1: point to the table idea "Start with 1 tricycle. How many wheels are left for the bicycles?" Q4: suggest drawing 4 friends and dealing out the stickers. Tutor rule at minute 59.5: if the clock is more than 2 minutes late, drop the last Core question of page 2 to take-home (children draw a star beside it). Never shorten talk time, the exit ticket, looking back or the closing. Questions marked with a star and the words take-home on the page are done at home; their answers are still on the check-together slide.

p2l3-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 73.5. Click each answer after a child explains. Q6: 3 rows does not work (3 rows of 6 is 18, 3 rows of 7 is 21). Think harder 1 (17 wheels): with 1 tricycle, 14 wheels are left: 7 bicycles. 2 tricycles leave 11, an odd number, which bicycles cannot make. 3 tricycles leave 8: 4 bicycles. 4 leave 5: no. 5 leave 2: 1 bicycle. 6 tricycles need 18 wheels: too many. So exactly 3 ways.

p2l3-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Open to any child who chooses it (the choice after question 3 on the worksheet). These are the SAME four questions as the printed Think harder page: the slide shows 1 to 3 and question 4 is on the page only. Never announce who is working on which page. Answers: 1) 3 ways: 7 bicycles and 1 tricycle (14 + 3); 4 bicycles and 3 tricycles (8 + 9); 1 bicycle and 5 tricycles (2 + 15). 0, 2 or 4 tricycles leave an odd number of wheels, which bicycles cannot make, and 6 or more tricycles need 18 wheels or more. 2) Siti is right: 5 hens and 4 goats (10 + 16 = 26). Mei cannot be right: every hen has 2 legs and every goat has 4 legs, so the total is always an even number, and 25 is odd. (Start with 9 hens, 18 legs; each swap to a goat adds 2: 18, 20, 22, 24, 26.) 3) 8 each (4 × 8 = 32) and 2 left over. 4) (Question: An array of stickers has 4 rows. Ben counts 12 stickers in the first 3 rows. How many stickers are in the whole array?) 16 stickers. 3 rows have 12, so each row has 4 (12 ÷ 3 = 4); 4 rows of 4 is 16.

p2l3-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Q6 and Q7 on the Think Harder page. Answers: 1) 27 sweets. 2) 5 hens and 3 goats.

p2l3-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? For Q1: "Which numbers from 21 to 29 leave 3 when we make groups of 4?" For Q2: "Try 1 goat. How many hens then?"

p2l3-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the 4 times table numbers from 20 to 28 are 20, 24, 28; add 3 to get 23, 27 (31 is too big). The 5 times table numbers are 20, 25; add 2 to get 22, 27. Only 27 is in both. Check: 27 = 6 fours + 3 = 5 fives + 2. Q2: keep the "2 more hens" rule in every guess, and change the number of goats by 1 each time. 5 hens and 3 goats: 10 + 12 = 22 legs.

p2l3-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then two volunteers share. Answer: No. If 4 or more were left, Ravi could give each friend one more, so the leftover is always 0, 1, 2 or 3. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Talk time rules: you choose volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"); never cold-call a child by name; any child may say pass; no public tallies, scores or rankings.

p2l3-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86.5. Answer: 3 hens and 2 goats (6 + 8 = 14 legs, 3 + 2 = 5 animals). Look for a table starting with 5 hens (10 legs). Extension: find all the arrays (at least 2 rows, at least 2 in each row) for 16 counters (3 ways: 2 rows of 8, 4 rows of 4, 8 rows of 2). Hold-up: children hold their slips up one at a time (never all together); the answer is on the next click. About 2 minutes of child work.

p2l3-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 88.5. Looking back: about 2 minutes, in the box on the page called "Before you go: Investigation and Looking back" (the page after worksheet page 2; every child reaches it). Children finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped. A pass is always allowed. No marks and no wrong answers. Tutor script: SAY: Looking back takes 2 minutes. Find the box called Looking back on the page “Before you go: Investigation and Looking back”. Finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped you. You may pass on any line. If you tick "I am still stuck", your tutor will check in during the session. DO: Nothing is collected in front of the group and nobody has to read theirs out. The tutor may read a box while stamping journals (never by private message), and checks in on a child who ticked still stuck during the open session, for example by a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal with a parent nearby, for example "I saw you drew it when you got stuck". A child may volunteer one sentence, never by name unless they choose to. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the next open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby). Praise the strategy, not the speed. Closing and stamps take the last minute and a half (88.5 to 90).
